content.text: Quick Write
Directions:
Complete your
Quick Write

to get ready for your final presentation. Write your planned opening sentence, explain how today’s lesson moves your presentation forward, and name one next step that will help your audience follow your ideas.
How does today’s work move your presentation forward, and what do you still need to do before you present?

In the previous lesson, students completed or refined their explanatory essays and process diagrams for the Gallery of Learning. Today, students turn that writing into a short presentation that teaches classmates how learning happens through effort, feedback, and practice. This helps students prepare for the performance task because they must explain their thinking clearly to a real audience.
Turn-and-Talk
Have students use the
Turn-and-Talk
routine to discuss the following prompt.
Students face a partner and keep their essay and process document nearby so they can connect today’s discussion to their own work.
Say these Directions:
Think about speeches, class presentations, or videos you have heard before.
Turn and talk
with your partner about what makes a presentation easy to follow and worth listening to.
Ask:
What makes a presentation clear and effective for an audience?

A clear presentation has a strong opening, a voice people can hear, and ideas in an order that makes sense. It also helps when the speaker looks up, uses a visual at the right time, and does not just read every word.
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:
Students, you have named audience-friendly speaking actions. Next you will learn how to notice those actions and use them in your own presentations.
Students will learn what makes a presentation clear, engaging, and easy to follow.
Noticing Strong Delivery Choices
Checklist Reviews
Have students get out their completed explanatory essays and process documents.
Teach:

When we present, the primary goal is to help our audience understand our ideas. A strong presenter makes purposeful choices about voice, pacing, eye contact, and visuals because those choices match the task, audience, and purpose. If I rush, mumble, or read every word, my audience has to work too hard. If I speak clearly and guide them through my ideas step by step, I make the learning easier to follow.
Display the lists of criteria for low- and high-quality presentations, and review them with the class. Then prepare to read Version A and Version B aloud.
Version A: Harder to Follow
The speaker:
speaks too quietly or too quickly
keeps eyes down instead of looking at audience
does not refer to the process diagram
moves from idea to idea without clear transitions
Version B: Easier to Follow
The speaker:
begins with a clear opening statement
speaks at a steady, easy-to-hear pace
uses sequence language to organize ideas
points to the process diagram while explaining stages
ends with a brief closing that restates the big idea
Say these Directions:

You will hear the same short presentation two times. As you listen, pay attention to the speaking choices that make the explanation easier or harder for the audience to understand. Think about the speaker’s voice, pacing, organization of ideas, and the use of the visual.
Version A:

Okay. My presentation is about Tree-ear learning how to make pottery. He watches Min and learns how to do the things that potters do. Then he starts helping and trying these things himself. He works hard and eventually gets better.
Version B:

My presentation explains how Tree-ear, a potter’s apprentice, develops skill through observation, practice, and feedback. First, he carefully watches Min, his mentor, create pottery from start to finish so that he can understand each step of the craft. Next, he begins helping with small tasks and practicing what he has observed. If you look at my process diagram, you can see how each stage builds on the one before it. In the end, Tree-ear’s efforts show that real skill develops through patience, practice and guidance.
Ask:
Which version helped you understand the idea better, and what specific speaking choices made the difference?

The second version was easier to understand because the speaker slowed down, used sequence words, and pointed to the process diagram at the right time. Those moves helped me follow each stage instead of hearing one long paragraph.
Support students in naming the language and delivery choices that make an oral presentation clear for listeners.
evaluation language
presentation vocabulary
cause-and-effect language for feedback
Allow a brief partner rehearsal in a shared home language or in mixed language before students give feedback in English, so they can clarify the idea first.
Affirm that students already know strong speaking from many settings, including family storytelling, coaching, explaining games, and teaching others a process.
Prompt students to name one exact delivery move before they explain its effect on the audience.
Encourage students to use language such as
clear opening, sequence words, pace, volume
, and
visual support
instead of vague comments, like
good
or
bad
You said, “She talked better” — we can explain that more clearly by saying: “Her pace was slower and clearer, so the audience could follow each step.”
That idea connects to audience understanding because the speaker used sequence language to organize the explanation.
Generative Oral/Language Supports (available to all students):
The stronger presentation was easier to follow because __________.
One delivery move that helped the audience was __________.
When the speaker __________, it made the explanation more clear.
Provide sentence frames for multilingual learners based on their proficiency levels as appropriate, and gradually reduce these supports as students become more independent.
Emerging:
Expanding:
"First, I will ___." / "Then, ___." / "Finally, ___."
Bridging:
"To begin, ___." / "Furthermore, ___." / "In conclusion, ___."
If students give only one-word judgments, such as “better” or “boring” → Prompt: "Name the exact speaking move you noticed. Was it the pace, the volume, the eye contact, or the use of the visual?"
If students focus only on confidence and not clarity → Prompt: "How did that choice help the audience understand the ideas, not just notice the speaker?"
Student names a specific delivery choice and explains its effect on the audience.
Student uses presentation language — such as
opening, pace, volume, visual
, or
sequence
— rather than general praise.

Students at different proficiency levels may need to begin at different points within the task. Based on responses, look for opportunities to support and expand student use of academic language, and provide scaffolding as needed.
Emerging:
Student uses a sequence frame, names 1–2 domain words from a bank, and speaks loudly and clearly.
Expanding:
Student uses sequence language and domain vocabulary and adjusts volume, pace, and eye contact for the audience.
Bridging:
Student uses precise sequence language and domain vocabulary; delivery matches the task, audience, and purpose.
Check for Understanding (SL.6.5, SL.6.6)
Pick two delivery moves that you want to use in your own presentation today. Write one sentence explaining why each move matters for your audience.
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:
You have identified the actions and words that make a presentation stronger. Now you will apply those same actions and words to your own Gallery Talk.

content.text: Situation
Try this
Struggling with: giving specific feedback
Offer a simple prompt: “Name one action you noticed. Then say how it helped the audience.”
Struggling with: identifying delivery choices
Limit the checklist to three focus categories for this rehearsal: voice, pacing, and use of the visual.
Struggling with: processing spoken language quickly
Repeat the second model once more, and pause briefly between ideas.
Struggling with: expressing ideas in writing
Allow students to give their two reasons orally to a partner or use speech-to-text for the CFU response.
Ready for extension

Ask students to explain which delivery choice mattered most for this specific task, and why. Invite students to compare the stronger model to a polished speech or presentation they know and identify one similar feature.
Students will evaluate presentation quality by noticing delivery choices connected to task, audience, and purpose.
Part A: Build Your Gallery Talk (SL.6.4.a)
(30 minutes)
Rehearse and Refine

Have students take out their completed essays and process documents. They will first work independently to create short speaking notes for their Gallery Talk presentation. Then they will exchange notes with a partner and use the Peer Review checklist to provide feedback on clarity and organization.
Say these Directions:
Take out your explanatory essay, your process document, and your
Peer Feedback
Form. On journal paper, you will be turning your writing into short speaking notes with four parts:
Opening
Key Idea 1
Key Idea 2
, and
Closing
Teach:

A presentation is not your whole essay spoken out loud. It is your clearest ideas, organized so a listener can follow them in real time. I look at my paragraph and keep the important ideas, but I shorten them into note phrases instead of full written sentences. Then I add sequence words like
prior to
subsequently
, and
from that point forward
so the audience can track the stages. Finally, I make sure my closing brings the listener back to the big idea.
Display the following teacher model of speaking notes, if needed for support and guidance:
Opening:
My presentation explains how Tree-ear develops skill through observation, practice, and feedback.
Prior to apprenticing formally:
He watches Min carefully and learns by noticing small details. (
Key Idea 1
Subsequently:
He completes simple tasks, makes mistakes, and keeps refining his work.
From that point forward:
His effort helps him connect craft to community and purpose. (
Key Idea 2
Closing:
Tree-ear’s journey shows that learning something difficult takes patience, guidance, and perseverance.
Ask:
How do the speaking notes help a presenter explain ideas clearly without reading the whole essay?
The speaking notes keep only the most important ideas. The presenter uses short phrases and sequence words so the audience can follow each key idea without hearing the whole essay read aloud.
Say these Directions:
Work on turning your writing into short speaking notes for the next eight minutes. Remember to use brief phrases to remind yourself of what to say rather than writing full sentences.
Once finished, exchange notes with your partner. Read each other's notes carefully. Use your Peer Feedback Form to share constructive feedback about your partner’s presentation notes.
When done, briefly read your partner’s comments and ask any questions you may have to clarify their feedback.
Display the Peer Review checklist:
Peer Review Checklist
Is the opening clear about the topic of the presentation?
Are there transition words to support moving from one idea to the next?
Are sequence words used to guide the audience?
Does the closing return to the big idea?
Are the notes short phrases rather than full sentences?
Peer Feedback
Comments
Suggestions
What is the main focus or argument?
Your main idea is that Tree-ear learns pottery through watching, practice, and feedback.
None, your opening sentence is good!
Ask clarifying questions.
I wondered how feedback helped Tree-ear get better.
Maybe an example of Min's feedback?
What are some key details?
You explained that Tree-ear watches Min, does small tasks, and gets better step-by-step.
Double-check the spelling and punctuation in your diagram.
Overall comments
Your notes are clear and easy to follow.
Maybe highlight the short notes?
Support students in transforming written explanations into concise oral language that listeners can follow.
sequence language
concise speaking notes
domain vocabulary for explanation
Affirm that students already know how to teach a process from everyday life; today they are transferring that skill to an academic audience.
Invite students to rehearse their explanation first in the language variety that helps them think most clearly before shaping it into academic English for the presentation.
Coach students to replace long written sentences with brief note phrases they can explain aloud.
Prompt students to keep one clear detail per stage rather than stacking too many facts into one point.
You said, “He learned by watching first and then doing stuff” — to clarify, we can say: “Prior to working independently, Tree-ear learned through careful observation and guided practice.”
You said, “Then he got better” — to clarify, we can say: “Subsequently, repeated practice and feedback helped him refine his skill.”
Generative Oral/Language Supports (available to all students):
My presentation will show that __________ develops through __________.
Prior to __________, the learner first __________.
Subsequently, __________, which shows __________.
From that point forward, __________ helped the learner grow.
If students copy whole essay sentences onto their notes → Prompt: "What is the shortest phrase that would remind you what to say aloud?"
If students list stages without explaining why they matter → Prompt: "Add one phrase after each stage that tells what it shows about learning."
Student organizes speaking notes with a clear beginning, middle, and end.
Student uses sequence language and domain vocabulary to make the stages of learning easy to follow.
Checklist
Check your work to ensure it:
includes only the most relevant ideas for a short class presentation rather than every detail from the essay
uses sequence language to move the audience through the stages of learning
includes domain vocabulary, such as
apprentice
mentor
refine
, and
persevere
uses your notes to support a spoken presentation with relevant facts and descriptive details

attrs.label: Additional Student Support: Creating Speaker’s Notes

content.text: Situation
Try this
Struggling with: condensing an essay into speaking notes
Tell students to choose only one strong detail for each stage in the process.
Struggling with: organizing ideas
Provide a spoken frame: opening, first stage, next stage, final idea.
Struggling with: starting the presentation
Offer a possible opening stem: My presentation explains how __________ grows through __________.
Struggling with: getting ideas onto paper
Allow students to sketch arrows from their process diagram and use speech-to-text or an oral rehearsal before writing notes.
Ready for extension

Ask students to add one purposeful gesture or visual cue to each stage of their presentation. Invite students to revise their closing so it connects both to Tree-ear’s growth and to the broader idea of craftsmanship in community.
Pulse Check (SL.6.4.a)
Which revision would best strengthen a short explanatory presentation for classmates?
Add every detail from the essay so nothing is left out.
Incorrect: A student may think more information always makes a presentation stronger, but too many details can make a short presentation hard to follow.
Read the essay exactly as written so the wording stays formal.
Incorrect: A student may think academic writing should be read word-for-word, but oral presentations need spoken language and clear pacing for listeners.
Organize the talk around the stages in the process diagram and explain each stage with one strong detail.
Correct: This revision matches the audience and purpose by using relevant facts, clear sequencing, and descriptive details.
Skip the visual and focus only on finishing quickly.
Incorrect: A student may focus on speed, but skipping the visual makes it harder for the audience to follow the explanation.

Students will turn their explanatory essays and process diagrams into short speaking notes, peer review each other’s work, and revise based on checklist-based feedback from classmates.

Quickwrite

Say these Directions:
Complete your
Quickwrite

to get ready for your final presentation. Write your planned opening sentence, explain how today’s lesson moves your presentation forward, and name one next step that will help your audience follow your ideas.
Ask:
How does today’s work move your presentation forward, and what do you still need to do before you present?

My work helped me shorten my notes so I can speak more naturally instead of reading my essay. My opening sentence is, “My presentation explains how Tree-ear grows from observer to skilled maker through patience, feedback, and practice.” Before I present, I still need to slow down during my second point and point to my process diagram when I explain how his work becomes more refined.

standards.description: Plan and deliver an informative/explanatory presentation that: develops a topic with relevant facts, definitions, and concrete details; uses appropriate transitions to clarify relationships; uses precise language and domain specific vocabulary; and provides a strong conclusion.

Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.
Follow rules for collegial discussions, set specific goals and deadlines, and define individual roles as needed.
Pose and respond to specific questions with elaboration and detail by making comments that contribute to the topic, text, or issue under discussion.
Review the key ideas expressed and demonstrate understanding of multiple perspectives through reflection and paraphrasing.
Include multimedia components (e.g., graphics, images, music, sound) and visual displays in presentations to clarify information.
Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.
Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information and evidence, paraphrasing key ideas, building on responses, and providing useful feedback.
Engage in conversational exchanges and express ideas on familiar topics by asking and answering yes‐no and wh‐ questions and responding using simple phrases.
Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information, and paraphrasing key ideas.

Use an expanded set of general academic words (e.g., affect, evidence, demonstrate, reluctantly), domain‐specific words (e.g., scene, setting, plot, point of view, fraction, cell membrane, democracy), synonyms, antonyms, and figurative language to create precision and shades of meaning while speaking and writing.
Use a select number of general academic words (e.g., author, chart) and domain‐specific words (e.g., scene, cell, fraction) to create some precision while speaking and writing.

Use a growing set of academic words (e.g., author, chart, global, affect), domain‐specific words (e.g., scene, setting, plot, point of view, fraction, cell membrane, democracy), synonyms, and antonyms to create precision and shades of meaning while speaking and writing.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations using appropriate register (e.g., to reflect on multiple perspectives) using a variety of learned phrases, indirect reported speech (e.g., I heard you say X, and Gabriel just pointed out Y), as well as open responses.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to gain and hold the floor or ask for clarification) using basic learned phrases (e.g., I think..., Would you please repeat that?), as well as open responses.
Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to provide counterarguments) using an expanded set of learned phrases (I agree with X, but...), as well as open responses.
Adjust language choices according to task (e.g., facilitating a science experiment, providing peer feedback on a writing assignment), purpose, task, and audience.
Adjust language choices according to social setting (e.g., classroom, break time) and audience (e.g., peers, teacher).
Adjust language choices according to purpose (e.g., explaining, persuading, entertaining), task, and audience.
Plan and deliver longer oral presentations on a variety of topics and content areas, using reasoning and evidence to support ideas, as well as growing understanding of register.
Plan and deliver brief oral presentations on a variety of topics and content areas.
Plan and deliver longer oral presentations on a variety of topics and content areas, using details and evidence to support ideas.
